aws-res-mcq-029.explanation: **The problem:** A license-bound app must run on exactly one instance (no ASG), but should auto-recover on hardware failure keeping its instance ID, private IP, and Elastic IP. **Why EC2 automatic recovery:** a CloudWatch alarm on `StatusCheckFailed_System` with the `recover` action migrates the instance to healthy hardware while preserving its identity — instance ID, private/Elastic IPs, and metadata — perfect for license-bound singletons (newer instance types enable simplified automatic recovery by default). **Why the distractors fail:** a second instance behind an ALB violates the single-instance constraint; manual AMI relaunch means downtime and a *new* identity; Spot capacity rebalancing is a Spot feature, not recovery. **The detail:** the recover action handles *system* status failures (host issues), not in-guest crashes. **Common mistakes:** using an ASG when licensing forbids it, and expecting recovery to fix instance (in-guest) status failures.
aws-res-mcq-029.example:
```bash
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name ec2-system-recover \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name StatusCheckFailed_System \
  --statistic Maximum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 --threshold 1 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:automate:us-east-1:ec2:recover
```

aws-res-mcq-030.explanation: **The problem:** On scale-in, terminated instances lose in-memory job state and unshipped logs — you need a drain window before termination. **Why a termination lifecycle hook:** it pauses the instance in `Terminating:Wait` between 'selected for termination' and 'terminated', fires a notification (EventBridge/SNS/SQS), and your script drains jobs and ships logs, then calls `complete-lifecycle-action` (or the timeout elapses). Launch hooks exist symmetrically for warm-up. **Why the distractors fail:** suspending the Terminate process or protecting every instance forever breaks scale-in entirely; the health-check grace period governs evaluation after *launch*, not termination. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to call `complete-lifecycle-action` (instance waits for the full timeout), and disabling scale-in instead of draining gracefully.
aws-res-mcq-030.example:
```bash
aws autoscaling put-lifecycle-hook \
  --auto-scaling-group-name worker-asg \
  --lifecycle-hook-name drain-on-terminate \
  --lifecycle-transition autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING \
  --heartbeat-timeout 300 --default-result CONTINUE
```

aws-res-mcq-031.explanation: **The problem:** During deployments users see errors as instances leave the ALB target group while still serving in-flight requests. **Why deregistration delay (connection draining):** when a target deregisters, the ALB immediately stops sending it *new* requests but keeps existing connections alive for the deregistration delay (default 300s) so in-flight requests complete — tune it to the longest expected request and deployment errors vanish. **Why the distractors fail:** idle timeout closes inactive connections (different concern); sticky sessions pin users to instances, making removal *worse*; cross-zone is about distribution, not draining. **Common mistakes:** setting the delay shorter than the longest request, and confusing idle timeout with deregistration delay.

aws-res-mcq-032.explanation: **The problem:** An app takes 4 minutes to initialize, but the ASG terminates brand-new instances as unhealthy before they finish booting — an infinite churn loop. **Why the health check grace period:** it tells the ASG how long to *ignore* health-check results after launch, giving slow-booting apps time to come up; set it above the real init time and instances are judged only once ready. **Why the distractors fail:** disabling checks removes self-healing; a *faster* ALB health-check interval makes the (premature) judgment come sooner; cooldown spacing governs scaling-activity pacing, not health evaluation after launch. **Common mistakes:** leaving the default grace period below the real boot time, and shortening health-check intervals to 'fix' the loop (it worsens it).

aws-res-mcq-033.explanation: **The problem:** A DynamoDB table must be restorable to any point in the last 35 days after accidental writes/deletes. **Why point-in-time recovery:** PITR maintains continuous backups, restorable to any second in the preceding 35 days — into a *new* table, from which you recover the data (on-demand backups complement it for long-term snapshots). **Why the distractors fail:** Streams capture change events for triggers (not a restore mechanism); global tables replicate corruption faithfully across Regions; DAX is a cache. **The exam vocabulary:** 'restore to any point in time' → PITR. **Common mistakes:** assuming Streams or global tables provide recovery, and forgetting PITR restores to a new table (not in place).

aws-res-mcq-034.explanation: **The problem:** A critical EFS file system needs a cross-Region copy kept current automatically, with minutes-level failover. **Why EFS replication:** it continuously replicates the file system to another Region (or AZ) with an RPO/RTO of minutes — managed, no agents or sync jobs — and for failover you stop replication and the replica becomes writable. **Why the distractors fail:** hand-rolled rsync from an instance is operational toil with hours of RPO; EBS snapshots don't apply to EFS; an EFS file system's mount targets exist only within its own Region (mounting cross-Region over peering is a latency trap, not DR). **Common mistakes:** scripting rsync for EFS DR, and trying to mount one EFS file system from another Region.

aws-res-mcq-035.explanation: **The problem:** You want DNS to return up to eight *healthy* IPs for clients to pick among, with unhealthy ones excluded — without paying for a load balancer. **Why multivalue answer routing:** it returns up to eight records, each individually health-checked — unhealthy IPs drop out of responses and clients spread across the rest. It's DNS-level pseudo-load-balancing: cheaper than an ELB but without connection awareness, draining, or instant failover (DNS TTL caching applies). **Why the distractors fail:** simple records with multiple values can't attach per-value health checks; failover is active-passive; weighted 100/0 sends everything to one target. **Common mistakes:** expecting ELB-grade behavior (no connection draining/instant failover at DNS), and using simple multi-value records that ignore health.

aws-res-mcq-036.explanation: **The problem:** A confirmation job must not be processed for at least 10 minutes (to allow cancellations) after it's sent. **Why a delay queue / message timers:** `DelaySeconds` on the queue (or per-message timers) hides a message from consumers for up to 15 minutes *from when it's sent* — exactly 'don't process before X'. **Why not visibility timeout:** that hides a message *after it's received*, governing retry windows — the exam's favorite confusion pair. **Why the distractors fail:** long polling waits at most 20 seconds; a FIFO queue orders messages but doesn't delay them. **Common mistakes:** using visibility timeout to delay *initial* delivery, and expecting delays longer than 15 minutes (use Step Functions wait states or EventBridge Scheduler instead).

aws-res-mcq-037.explanation: **The problem:** Direct Connect carries critical traffic and needs a cost-effective failover path if the circuit drops. **Why a Site-to-Site VPN backup over the internet:** BGP prefers the DX path while it's healthy and routing fails over to the IPsec VPN when the circuit fails — lower bandwidth, but connectivity survives, at low cost. **Why the distractors fail:** a second DX through the *same* provider/location shares failure modes and costs far more (appropriate only when bandwidth must also survive, via *separate* locations); a single DX has no built-in redundancy; Transfer Acceleration is an S3 upload feature. **Common mistakes:** assuming DX is inherently redundant, and buying a second co-located DX when a VPN backup meets the cost-effective failover need.

aws-res-mr-007.explanation: **The problem:** You want canary releases on an ALB — shift a small % of live traffic to a new version, watch error rates, then continue or roll back instantly. **Why the two answers:** deploy the new version to a *separate* target group (green) alongside the current one (blue), and use ALB *weighted target groups* to shift traffic gradually (1% → 10% → 100%, or back to 0% instantly on errors — the rollback is a weight change, not a redeploy). **Why both:** two independently routable environments + weighted routing = blue/green with canary. **Why the distractors fail:** in-place instance replacement has no rollback path and mixes versions in one pool; health-threshold and instance-size changes don't direct traffic between versions. **Common mistakes:** rolling instances in place (no instant rollback), and conflating health checks with traffic shifting.

aws-res-mcq-038.explanation: **The problem:** SQS messages must be processed by Lambda, auto-scaling with queue depth, batching, returning failures to the queue — with no poller to manage. **Why an event source mapping:** it's Lambda's managed poller — it long-polls the queue, invokes the function with batches, scales pollers up/down with traffic, and leaves failed batches (or items, with partial batch responses) to reappear per the queue's redrive policy. **Why the distractors fail:** a scheduled poller adds latency and fixed cadence; SNS inverts the pattern and drops the buffering; an EC2 poller fleet is exactly the infrastructure this feature eliminates. **Common mistakes:** building a custom poller, and not enabling partial batch responses (so one bad message fails the whole batch).
aws-res-mcq-038.example:
```bash
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
  --function-name process-orders \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:123456789012:orders \
  --batch-size 10 \
  --function-response-types ReportBatchItemFailures
```

resources.label: AWS — Lambda with SQS (event source mapping)

aws-res-mcq-039.explanation: **The problem:** A small team wants containers with AWS handling servers entirely, tasks auto-restarted, and a service maintaining desired count. **Why ECS services on Fargate:** Fargate is serverless container compute — no instances to patch, size, or scale — and an ECS *service* adds the resilience contract: it monitors tasks, replaces failures, maintains desired count across AZs, and integrates load-balancer health checks. **Why the distractors fail:** the EC2 launch type reintroduces fleet management; one big Docker host is a single point of failure; Lambda suits short functions, not arbitrary long-running containers. **Common mistakes:** choosing the EC2 launch type when 'no servers to manage' is the requirement, and running containers on a single host.

aws-res-mcq-040.explanation: **The problem:** In-place SSH patching causes configuration drift and mysterious incidents. **Why immutable infrastructure:** every change produces a new artifact (AMI / launch-template version) and deployment means *replacing* instances — ASG instance refresh rolls the fleet gradually with health checks — so drift becomes impossible (servers are reproducible from the artifact) and rollback is redeploying the previous version. **Why the distractors fail:** stricter SSH approval and quarterly audits *manage* drift but don't remove its mechanism; bigger instances just change less often (drift still accrues). **The principle:** don't modify running servers — rebuild and replace. **Common mistakes:** patching in place and auditing for drift, instead of baking immutable images.

aws-res-mr-008.explanation: **The problem:** A mistaken script nearly deleted a production RDS database. **Why the two answers (defense in depth):** deletion protection makes `DeleteDBInstance` fail outright until the flag is deliberately removed (a separate, conscious step), and automated backups guarantee point-in-time recovery if data is lost anyway. **Why both:** one prevents the delete; the other recovers if something slips through. **Why the distractors actively reduce safety:** wider `rds:DeleteDBInstance` permissions, skipping the final snapshot, and disabling Multi-AZ all make things worse. **The complement:** IAM least privilege on delete actions. **Common mistakes:** relying on a single control, and granting broad delete permissions 'for accountability'.

aws-res-mcq-041.explanation: **The problem:** Bursts from API clients overwhelm a backend; you want API Gateway to reject excess with HTTP 429 *before* the backend, with different limits per consumer. **Why throttling + usage plans + API keys:** API Gateway throttles with a token bucket (rate + burst) at account, stage, method, and — via *usage plans with API keys* — per-consumer levels, returning 429 when exceeded, so the backend only ever sees in-contract traffic and noisy clients can't starve others. **Why the distractors fail:** a larger backend pays for abuse; documentation isn't enforcement; API Gateway doesn't embed an SQS queue (that's a separate integration pattern). **Common mistakes:** scaling the backend instead of throttling at the edge, and treating client-side guidelines as a control.
aws-res-mcq-041.example:
```bash
aws apigateway create-usage-plan \
  --name premium \
  --throttle burstLimit=200,rateLimit=100 \
  --quota limit=1000000,period=MONTH
```

resources.label: AWS — API Gateway throttling & usage plans

aws-res-mcq-042.explanation: **The problem:** What happens when an Aurora cluster's writer fails? **Why automatic promotion:** Aurora replicas share the same distributed storage volume as the writer, so promotion needs no data copying — failover typically completes in under 30 seconds, choosing the candidate by failover *priority tier* (0–15, lower first, then largest instance). The cluster endpoint follows the new writer automatically; apps just reconnect. **Why no data loss:** storage is six copies across three AZs. **Why the distractors fail:** it doesn't stay read-only awaiting an admin; no data is lost; the endpoint doesn't need manual repointing. **The nuance:** with *no* replica, Aurora recreates the writer instead, which is slower. **Common mistakes:** assuming manual intervention is needed, and not configuring failover priority tiers for the preferred target.

aws-perf-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** A single EBS volume must sustain 60,000 consistent IOPS for a database. **Why io2 Provisioned IOPS SSD:** it's designed for high, *consistent* random IOPS — up to 64,000 on Nitro instances (more with io2 Block Express) — exactly the database pattern. **Why the distractors fail:** gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS per volume; the HDD families (st1 throughput-optimized, sc1 cold) are for sequential throughput workloads (logs, cold data), not random IOPS. **The exam skill:** match volume type to the IOPS/throughput requirement — random IOPS → io1/io2, throughput → st1, cheap cold → sc1, general → gp3. **Common mistakes:** picking gp3 for >16,000 IOPS, and using HDD for a random-access database.

aws-perf-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** Global users get slow loads for images/videos served from an S3 bucket in one Region. **Why CloudFront:** it caches the content at hundreds of edge locations close to users — one distribution with the bucket as origin, no application changes, no replication to manage. **Why the distractors fail:** multi-Region replication with per-user URLs reinvents a CDN at far higher cost/complexity; relocating the bucket helps one geography at others' expense; versioning is unrelated to latency. **The pattern:** 'global users, static/cacheable content, reduce latency simply' → CloudFront. **Common mistakes:** hand-rolling regional copies instead of using a CDN, and moving the origin (helps some users, hurts others).

aws-perf-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** A multiplayer game uses custom UDP, needs lowest global latency to servers in two Regions, and clients must connect to fixed IPs. **Why Global Accelerator:** it provides two static anycast IPs and routes *any* TCP/UDP traffic onto the AWS backbone from the nearest edge, with automatic failover between Regional endpoints — built for non-HTTP, latency-sensitive workloads (gaming, VoIP, IoT). **Why the distractors fail:** CloudFront accelerates HTTP(S) content/APIs, not custom UDP; Route 53 latency routing picks a Region at DNS time but gives no static IPs or backbone routing; ALBs are HTTP-layer and Regional. **The discriminator:** static IPs + non-HTTP + global low latency → Global Accelerator. **Common mistakes:** choosing CloudFront for UDP, and assuming DNS routing equals backbone acceleration.

aws-perf-mcq-004.explanation: **The problem:** A read-heavy DynamoDB app needs microsecond reads for hot items with minimal code change. **Why DAX:** DynamoDB Accelerator is a purpose-built, API-compatible in-memory cache — point the SDK at the DAX endpoint and reads drop from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds, with write-through caching and *no* cache-aside logic to write. **Why the distractors fail:** ElastiCache reaches similar latency but you build/maintain the caching layer and cache-aside code; global tables address multi-Region access, not single-Region read latency; more RCUs raise throughput but never break the millisecond floor. **The signal:** 'DynamoDB + microseconds + minimal change' → DAX. **Common mistakes:** adding RCUs to fix latency (it fixes throughput), and hand-building ElastiCache when DAX is drop-in.

aws-perf-mcq-005.explanation: **The problem:** A service needs millions of TCP connections/sec at ultra-low latency, and partners must whitelist fixed IPs per AZ. **Why NLB:** it operates at layer 4 — millions of requests/sec, extreme low latency, and uniquely a *static IP* (or your own Elastic IP) per AZ, which satisfies partner whitelisting. **Why the distractors fail:** ALB is layer 7 with DNS-name addressing and changing IPs (no static IP to whitelist); Classic LB is legacy; Route 53 weighting isn't a load balancer and offers no health-aware connection handling at this scale. **The discriminator:** static IP + extreme TCP throughput/low latency → NLB; HTTP routing/features → ALB. **Common mistakes:** choosing ALB when fixed IPs are required, and using DNS weighting as a load balancer.

aws-perf-mr-001.explanation: **The problem:** RDS PostgreSQL slows under read-heavy traffic — repeated product queries plus heavy analytics scans. **Why the two answers (complementary read scaling):** an ElastiCache cluster absorbs the *repeated identical* reads (product pages) at sub-millisecond latency, while read replicas absorb the *heavy, varied* reads (analytics) without touching the primary. **Why both:** caching kills duplicate hot reads; replicas offload the rest. **Why the distractors fail:** Multi-AZ is availability, not performance; backups don't serve queries; one bigger instance is vertical scaling with a ceiling and a single point of failure. **Common mistakes:** using Multi-AZ to offload reads, and vertically scaling instead of caching + replicas.

aws-perf-mcq-006.explanation: **The problem:** 100k clickstream events/sec, multiple independent apps must read the *same* events in order, and analysts need 24-hour replay. **Why Kinesis Data Streams:** it supports many consumers reading the same records (vs SQS where consumers compete and deleting removes data for everyone), per-shard ordering, and replay within the retention window (24h–365d). **Why the distractors fail:** SNS pushes but doesn't retain or replay; Step Functions orchestrates workflows, not ingestion; SQS is for competing-consumer queues, not shared replayable streams. **The signature:** 'multiple consumers + replay + ordering' → Kinesis. **Common mistakes:** choosing SQS for multi-consumer broadcast, and forgetting replay needs a stream, not a queue.

aws-perf-mcq-007.explanation: **The problem:** Analysts want occasional ad-hoc SQL over CSV/JSON in S3 with no servers and no loading. **Why Athena:** it's serverless, queries data *in place* in S3 with standard SQL, and bills per data scanned — the definition of occasional ad-hoc analysis. **Why the distractors fail:** RDS and Redshift require loading the data and running (and paying for) always-on infrastructure; EMR suits heavy custom big-data processing, not casual SQL. **The mapping:** 'serverless SQL over S3' → Athena. **Common mistakes:** standing up a database/cluster for occasional queries, and using EMR when plain SQL suffices.

aws-perf-mcq-008.explanation: **The problem:** Athena over a growing lake of CSV is slow and expensive. **Why convert to partitioned, columnar Parquet (via Glue ETL):** columnar Parquet lets Athena read only the queried columns, and partitioning (e.g. by date) prunes whole directories — together routinely cutting scanned bytes (the cost driver) by 10–100×. **Why Glue:** it's the managed ETL service for the CSV→Parquet transformation. **Why the distractors fail:** S3 buckets have no size tiers; Athena has no instance sizes; ZIP isn't a splittable, query-friendly format (and Athena still scans it). **Common mistakes:** querying raw CSV at scale, and compressing without converting to a columnar format.

aws-perf-mcq-009.explanation: **The problem:** A tightly-coupled HPC workload needs the lowest possible inter-node latency. **Why a cluster placement group (single AZ):** it packs instances close together on the same high-bisection-bandwidth network segment — lowest latency, highest throughput — the HPC choice (often paired with Elastic Fabric Adapter for MPI). **Why the distractors fail:** spread placement maximizes *separation* for a few critical instances; partition placement isolates groups for large distributed systems (Kafka/HDFS); separate Regions multiply latency. **The mapping:** lowest latency/tight coupling → cluster; max isolation → spread; fault-isolated partitions → partition. **Common mistakes:** using spread/partition for latency-sensitive HPC, and spanning AZs/Regions for a tightly-coupled job.

aws-perf-mcq-010.explanation: **The problem:** A CPU-bound Lambda (already efficient code) is too slow. **Why increase memory:** Lambda exposes one performance dial — memory (128 MB–10 GB) — and vCPU scales *linearly* with it (about 6 vCPUs at the top). More memory = more CPU; there's no separate CPU setting. **Why the distractors fail:** a longer timeout lets slow work finish but doesn't speed it up; provisioned concurrency removes cold starts (a start-latency concern, not per-invocation compute); there is no dedicated-vCPU configuration. **The exam skill:** sizing Lambda = choosing memory. **Common mistakes:** raising the timeout to 'go faster', and looking for a vCPU knob that doesn't exist.

aws-perf-mcq-011.explanation: **The problem:** An in-memory analytics engine needs a high RAM:vCPU ratio. **Why the R family:** instance family letters map to resource profiles — R (and X/z for extremes) = memory optimized for in-memory databases and analytics. **Why the distractors fail:** C = compute optimized (CPU-bound work); T = burstable general purpose (spiky light workloads); I = storage optimized (high local NVMe IOPS). **The exam quick-win:** match workload shape to family — memory → R/X, CPU → C, burst → T, local storage → I, GPU → P/G. **Common mistakes:** defaulting to general-purpose M when a memory-optimized R fits, and confusing storage-optimized I with memory-optimized R.

aws-perf-mcq-012.explanation: **The problem:** A one-time 200 TB NFS→S3 migration over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link, with verification and scheduling. **Why DataSync:** it's the online bulk-transfer service — an agent reads NFS/SMB, saturates available bandwidth with parallelism, verifies integrity, and supports scheduled or one-time jobs. **Why online is fine here:** 200 TB over 10 Gbps is a few days — well within reason. **Why the distractors fail:** File Gateway is for *ongoing hybrid access* (local cache, S3 backing), not migrations; Transfer Acceleration speeds *internet* uploads (irrelevant over DX); Snowball is the *offline* option when the network would take too long. **Common mistakes:** reaching for Snowball when the link is fast enough, and using File Gateway for a one-time migration.

aws-perf-mr-002.explanation: **The problem:** Global field teams upload multi-GB videos to one S3 bucket; uploads are slow and restart from zero on drops. **Why the two answers:** multipart upload parallelizes parts and retries only failed parts — a dropped connection no longer restarts gigabytes (recommended >100 MB, required >5 GB) — and S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads into the nearest CloudFront edge and across the AWS backbone, fixing the long-haul internet leg. **Why both:** multipart fixes reliability + parallelism; Transfer Acceleration fixes the global distance. **Why the distractors fail:** versioning and storage classes don't affect transfer speed; single PUTs with a longer timeout are exactly what's failing. **Common mistakes:** uploading large files as one PUT, and ignoring the long-haul network for global uploaders.

resources.label: AWS — S3 multipart upload & Transfer Acceleration

aws-perf-mcq-013.explanation: **The problem:** Real-time leaderboards (sorted rankings) need an in-memory store with replication, automatic failover, and persistence options. **Why ElastiCache for Redis:** Redis sorted sets are purpose-built for leaderboards, and it supports replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, snapshots/AOF persistence, and pub/sub. **Why the distractors fail:** Memcached is simpler (multithreaded, easy scale-out) but has *no* replication, persistence, or rich data structures; DynamoDB isn't in-memory; RDS with a big buffer pool is still a disk-based relational DB. **The exam split:** rich data types/replication/persistence → Redis; simple, multithreaded cache → Memcached. **Common mistakes:** choosing Memcached when HA/persistence/sorted-sets are required.

aws-perf-mcq-014.explanation: **The problem:** A DynamoDB table keyed on `status` (only ACTIVE/INACTIVE) throttles despite huge provisioned capacity. **Why hot partitions:** DynamoDB hashes the partition key to spread data and throughput across partitions; with only two key values, nearly all traffic lands on two partitions — each capped at ~3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU — so the table throttles while aggregate capacity sits idle. **The fix:** a *high-cardinality* partition key (user ID, order ID), possibly with write sharding. **Why the distractors fail:** sort keys and GSIs don't repair a degenerate partition-key choice; capacity is per-table/partition, not per item. **Common mistakes:** choosing a low-cardinality partition key, and adding capacity to fix a key-design problem.

aws-perf-mcq-015.explanation: **The problem:** Continuous SQS polling mostly returns empty, driving up API cost and CPU. **Why long polling:** setting `ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds` (up to 20s) holds the receive call open until a message arrives or the wait expires — eliminating the empty-response storm, cutting API calls (cost), and *reducing* delivery latency versus sleeping. **Why the distractors fail:** a 5-minute sleep adds up to 5 minutes of latency; FIFO changes ordering, not polling; visibility timeout governs in-flight invisibility, not polling. **The pairing:** empty receives/cost → long polling. **Common mistakes:** sleeping between polls (adds latency), and confusing visibility timeout with poll wait time.

resources.label: AWS — SQS short vs long polling

aws-perf-mcq-016.explanation: **The problem:** A Lambda API shows 1–2s latency on the first request after idle, then 50ms — cold starts. **Why provisioned concurrency:** it keeps a configured number of execution environments initialized and warm, so requests hit pre-warmed instances at steady latency (apply it to the production alias/version). **Why the distractors fail:** more memory speeds *execution* but not initialization; *reserved* concurrency is a limit/guarantee on concurrent executions — a different knob with a confusingly similar name (classic distractor); container images generally cold-start slower, not faster. **The distinction:** cold-start latency → provisioned concurrency; concurrency limits → reserved concurrency. **Common mistakes:** confusing reserved vs provisioned concurrency, and adding memory to fix cold starts.

aws-perf-mcq-017.explanation: **The problem:** Distributed ML training on hundreds of instances needs a shared POSIX file system with sub-ms latency and hundreds of GB/s aggregate throughput, sourced from S3. **Why FSx for Lustre:** it's the HPC/ML parallel file system — hundreds of GB/s, sub-millisecond latency, with an S3 data repository association that lazy-loads from and writes back to S3. **Why the distractors fail:** EFS is general-purpose NFS (solid but not in Lustre's performance class for this pattern); Mountpoint for S3 suits sequential object access, not POSIX random I/O; one instance re-exporting EBS over NFS bottlenecks the whole cluster. **The mapping:** HPC/ML high-throughput POSIX + S3 → FSx for Lustre. **Common mistakes:** using EFS for extreme-throughput HPC, and single-node NFS re-export.

aws-perf-mcq-018.explanation: **The problem:** A Windows app needs shared SMB storage with Active Directory integration and NTFS permissions. **Why FSx for Windows File Server:** it's a fully managed native Windows file system — SMB protocol, NTFS, DFS namespaces, and AD integration (AWS Managed AD or self-managed). **Why the distractors fail:** EFS speaks NFS (Linux territory); S3 is object storage, not a file share; FSx for Lustre targets Linux HPC. **The tell is the protocol:** SMB/AD → FSx for Windows; NFS/Linux → EFS; parallel HPC → Lustre. **Common mistakes:** using EFS for a Windows/SMB workload, and treating S3 as a mountable file share.

resources.label: AWS — FSx for Windows File Server

aws-perf-mcq-019.explanation: **The problem:** App logs must stream into S3 (and optionally Redshift) in near real time, with optional Lambda transform — and zero servers, shards, or consumers to manage. **Why Kinesis Data Firehose:** it's the fully managed delivery pipe — batches, optionally transforms (Lambda) and converts formats, and delivers to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and third parties, scaling automatically with no shards or consumers. **Why the distractors fail:** Kinesis Data Streams needs custom consumers/shard sizing (the right pick when you need replay or custom real-time processing); SQS+workers is hand-built; DataSync moves file systems, not streams. **The mapping:** 'easiest way to load streaming data into a store' → Firehose. **Common mistakes:** choosing Data Streams when no custom consumer/replay is needed, and building worker fleets.

aws-perf-mcq-020.explanation: **The problem:** Complex aggregations joining billions of rows for BI take minutes on RDS PostgreSQL. **Why Redshift:** this is OLAP — scanning/aggregating huge datasets — and Redshift's columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing are built for it, routinely turning minutes into seconds at petabyte scale. **Why the distractors fail:** RDS is row-oriented OLTP (scaling it up only delays the wall); DynamoDB serves key-based access, not ad-hoc joins; ElastiCache accelerates repeated reads, not novel analytical queries. **Core vocabulary:** OLTP → RDS; OLAP/data warehouse → Redshift. **Common mistakes:** scaling RDS for analytics, and using a key-value store for ad-hoc joins.

aws-perf-mcq-021.explanation: **The problem:** Product search needs full-text queries, fuzzy typo matching, filters, and relevance ranking. **Why OpenSearch Service:** it's the managed search engine (Elasticsearch fork) — inverted indexes for full-text search, fuzzy matching, faceted filtering, and relevance scoring out of the box. **Why the distractors fail:** SQL `LIKE '%term%'` can't use indexes and has no ranking; DynamoDB scans are expensive full reads with no text awareness; Athena is batch SQL over S3, not an interactive search backend. **The mapping:** full-text/relevance search → OpenSearch. **Common mistakes:** building search on SQL `LIKE`, and using DynamoDB scans for text search.

aws-perf-mr-003.explanation: **The problem:** A tightly-coupled simulation is bottlenecked by inter-node network latency/throughput. **Why the two answers:** instance types with enhanced networking (ENA, and EFA for MPI-style HPC) raise per-instance packet rates and lower latency, while a cluster placement group in one AZ physically co-locates the fleet on a low-latency, high-bisection segment. **Why both:** the NIC capability + the physical placement together maximize node-to-node performance. **Why the distractors fail:** spreading across Regions multiplies latency by orders of magnitude; EBS is storage, not network; an ALB is an HTTP front door, not an inter-node fabric. **Common mistakes:** spanning AZs/Regions for a tightly-coupled job, and adding storage/load-balancers to a network-bound problem.

aws-perf-mcq-022.explanation: **The problem:** An Aurora cluster (writer + 4 replicas) should spread reads across all replicas automatically, including future auto-scaled ones. **Why the reader endpoint:** it load-balances connections across all *current* read replicas — replicas added/removed by auto scaling join and leave automatically, with no application changes. **Why the distractors fail:** the cluster endpoint always targets the *writer* (use it for writes); hand-rolled rotation over instance endpoints breaks whenever the replica set changes; raw IPs break on failover. **The pairing:** reads → reader endpoint; writes → cluster endpoint. **Common mistakes:** sending reads to the cluster endpoint, and managing replica connections manually.

aws-perf-mcq-023.explanation: **The problem:** Identical GET requests hammer a Lambda backend behind API Gateway for catalog data that changes every few minutes. **Why API Gateway caching:** stage-level caching stores responses keyed by request (configurable per method and by parameters), serving repeats from cache until the TTL expires — Lambda invocation count (and cost) collapses. Matching the TTL to the change cadence (a few minutes) keeps staleness acceptable. **Why the distractors fail:** more concurrency or memory just processes the redundant invocations faster; switching to EC2 doesn't remove the redundancy. **Common mistakes:** scaling the backend to absorb repeated identical reads, and setting a TTL longer than the data's freshness tolerance.

aws-perf-mcq-024.explanation: **The problem:** A job needs scratch space with millions of IOPS and microsecond latency for temporary files worthless after completion. **Why NVMe instance store:** it's physically attached NVMe — no network hop — delivering millions of IOPS and microsecond latency that even io2 Block Express (network-attached) can't match. Its catch is ephemerality: data is lost on stop/terminate, which is exactly fine for scratch. **Why the distractors fail:** io2 is network-attached (lower ceiling); EFS adds network/NFS overhead; S3 is object storage, not low-latency scratch. **The pattern:** temporary/scratch + extreme IOPS → instance store; persistent + high IOPS → io2. **Common mistakes:** using instance store for data that must survive, and expecting io2 to match local NVMe latency.

aws-perf-mcq-025.explanation: **The problem:** A cache-aside (lazy-loading) ElastiCache setup serves stale data for a long time after updates. **Why add write-through:** lazy loading populates the cache only on read *misses*, so an updated row stays stale until its cached copy expires — write-through complements it by updating the cache on every database *write*, so reads always see current data. **The classic combo:** write-through + lazy loading + a TTL safety net (TTL bounds staleness for anything written by paths that bypass the cache). **Why the distractors fail:** connection timeouts, caching misses, and the engine choice change failure behavior/memory/engine — not freshness. **Common mistakes:** relying on lazy loading alone for write-heavy data, and omitting a TTL safety net.

aws-perf-mcq-026.explanation: **The problem:** 60 VPCs across accounts plus Direct Connect — full-mesh peering is unmanageable. **Why Transit Gateway:** it's the regional network hub — VPCs, VPN connections, and Direct Connect gateways attach once, and hub route tables control who reaches whom (thousands of attachments, cross-Region peering available). **Why the distractors fail:** a 60-VPC full mesh needs ~1,770 peering connections, and peering isn't transitive — exactly the wall hit here; PrivateLink exposes specific *services*, not whole networks; a NAT gateway is internet egress. **The mapping:** many-VPC hub-and-spoke → Transit Gateway. **Common mistakes:** scaling peering instead of adopting a hub, and expecting peering to be transitive.

aws-perf-mcq-027.explanation: **The problem:** Daily large transfers over an internet VPN miss deadlines because bandwidth fluctuates. **Why Direct Connect:** it's a dedicated physical circuit (1/10/100 Gbps or hosted capacities) between the data center and AWS — bandwidth and latency are *consistent* because traffic never crosses the public internet. **Why the distractors fail:** a second VPN tunnel still rides the internet (same variability); Transfer Acceleration helps S3 uploads over the internet but guarantees nothing; bigger receiving instances don't fix the pipe. **The mapping:** consistent/dedicated bandwidth to AWS → Direct Connect. **Common mistakes:** adding VPN tunnels to fix internet variability, and confusing Transfer Acceleration with dedicated connectivity.

aws-perf-mcq-028.explanation: **The problem:** A CloudFront site runs A/B tests — route to one of two origins based on a cookie, at the edge, with no round trip to a Region. **Why Lambda@Edge (origin request):** it runs at CloudFront locations on viewer/origin request and response events; an *origin-request* function can inspect the cookie and rewrite the origin per request — the canonical A/B mechanism. **The sibling:** CloudFront Functions are lighter/cheaper for sub-millisecond header/URL rewrites on *viewer* events, but origin selection lives with Lambda@Edge. **Why the distractors fail:** geo restrictions block countries; Route 53 weights split by DNS query (blind to cookies); S3 redirect rules can't read cookies. **Common mistakes:** using CloudFront Functions for origin selection, and trying cookie logic in Route 53.

aws-perf-mcq-029.explanation: **The problem:** Nightly Spark jobs over terabytes from S3, with AWS managing the cluster and Spot for workers. **Why EMR:** it's managed big-data infrastructure — clusters running Spark/Hadoop/Hive/Presto reading straight from S3 (EMRFS), with deep Spot integration for task nodes; *transient* clusters that exist only for the nightly run are the cost-efficient pattern. **Why the distractors fail:** Lambda caps at 15 minutes and 10 GB (wrong shape for terabyte Spark); RDS is a relational database; QuickSight visualizes results, it doesn't compute them. **The mapping:** managed Spark/Hadoop big-data processing → EMR. **Common mistakes:** forcing big-data jobs into Lambda, and running always-on clusters for nightly batches.

aws-perf-mcq-030.explanation: **The problem:** Hundreds of thousands of containerized jobs with varied resources and dependencies, needing managed queues, right-sized provisioning, and Spot — without building a scheduler. **Why AWS Batch:** it's purpose-built batch scheduling — job definitions, priority queues, dependencies, array jobs for massive parallelism, and compute environments that provision optimal EC2/Spot/Fargate capacity per demand. **Why the distractors fail:** Step Functions orchestrates workflows (and often *submits* Batch jobs) but isn't a queue/packing scheduler; SQS+workers means building Batch yourself; Lambda's 15-min/10 GB limits don't fit heavy jobs. **The mapping:** large-scale batch/HPC job scheduling → AWS Batch. **Common mistakes:** hand-building a scheduler on SQS, and confusing workflow orchestration with batch scheduling.

aws-perf-mcq-031.explanation: **The problem:** Interactive BI dashboards over Athena/Redshift for hundreds of users, with ML insights and no BI servers. **Why QuickSight:** it's the serverless BI service — native connectors to Athena, Redshift, RDS, and S3, the in-memory SPICE engine for fast interactive queries, per-session reader pricing, embedding, and ML insights (anomaly detection, forecasting). **Why the distractors fail:** CloudWatch dashboards visualize *metrics*; Glue DataBrew is data preparation; OpenSearch Dashboards serve log/search analytics on OpenSearch data. **The mapping:** managed BI/visualization → QuickSight. **Common mistakes:** using CloudWatch dashboards for business BI, and confusing data prep (DataBrew) with visualization.

aws-perf-mcq-032.explanation: **The problem:** 'Friends of friends who like hiking' across billions of relationships in milliseconds — relational JOINs are unusable. **Why Neptune:** it's the managed graph database — property graphs (Gremlin/openCypher) and RDF (SPARQL) — built to traverse relationship networks in milliseconds where the equivalent SQL needs explosive self-JOINs. Social graphs, recommendations, fraud rings, and knowledge graphs are its signature scenarios. **Why the distractors fail:** Redshift aggregates columns, DynamoDB serves key-value at scale, ElastiCache caches — none traverse relationships natively. **The mapping:** highly-connected relationship queries → Neptune. **Common mistakes:** modeling graph traversals as SQL self-JOINs, and using DynamoDB for relationship-heavy queries.

aws-perf-mcq-033.explanation: **The problem:** An io2 volume provisioned for 40,000 IOPS never exceeds ~20,000 while the app is I/O starved, with no volume queue saturation. **Why the instance is the bottleneck:** EBS performance is min(volume, instance) — every instance type has its own EBS-attached IOPS/throughput ceiling, and a c5.large caps far below 40,000 IOPS, so the volume is fine but the instance can't drive it. The fix is a larger size (or an EBS-optimized family with higher EBS bandwidth). **Why the distractors fail:** io2 exceeds 64,000 IOPS; RAID 1 mirrors for redundancy (it halves write throughput); Multi-Attach is about multiple instances, not speed. **Common mistakes:** blaming the volume when the instance's EBS ceiling is the cap, and adding RAID 1 hoping for speed.

aws-perf-mcq-034.explanation: **The problem:** Backup software expects an iSCSI virtual tape interface; the company wants to retire tape hardware and store backups in S3/Glacier without changing the software. **Why Tape Gateway:** it presents a virtual tape library (VTL) over iSCSI, so existing backup software (Veeam, NetBackup, Commvault) keeps working unchanged — virtual tapes land in S3 and 'ejected' tapes archive to Glacier tiers. **Why the distractors fail:** File Gateway is NFS/SMB to S3; DataSync migrates files; EBS snapshots don't speak to backup software. **The Storage Gateway map:** File = NFS/SMB→S3, Volume = iSCSI block, Tape = VTL. **Common mistakes:** confusing the gateway types, and trying to point tape backup software at File Gateway.

aws-perf-mcq-035.explanation: **The problem:** Move 600 TB to S3 within three weeks over a non-upgradeable 200 Mbps uplink. **Why Snowball Edge (do the math first):** 600 TB over 200 Mbps ≈ 280+ days at full saturation — no online method (DataSync, Transfer Acceleration, multipart) beats the arithmetic of the pipe. Snowball Edge devices hold ~80 TB usable each; several in parallel, loaded locally and shipped back, complete the transfer within the deadline. **Why the distractors fail:** every online option is bounded by the same 200 Mbps. **The rule of thumb:** when transfer time exceeds ~a week of dedicated bandwidth, go offline. **Common mistakes:** skipping the bandwidth math, and assuming Transfer Acceleration/DataSync can overcome a slow uplink.

aws-perf-mcq-036.explanation: **The problem:** 10 GB S3 downloads are far slower than available bandwidth on a single stream, and a network blip restarts the whole file. **Why parallel byte-range GETs:** the `Range` header lets each request pull a slice of the object; running slices concurrently aggregates throughput far beyond one TCP stream, and a failed slice retries alone instead of restarting 10 GB. It's the download mirror of multipart upload (SDK transfer managers do both automatically). **Why the distractors fail:** storage class doesn't change wire speed; a bigger archive worsens the retry problem; a NAT gateway adds cost, not bandwidth. **Common mistakes:** single-stream downloads of huge objects, and combining files into one archive (bigger restart on failure).
aws-perf-mcq-036.example:
```bash
# Fetch a byte range; run several of these concurrently for one object
aws s3api get-object --bucket my-bucket --key big.bin \
  --range bytes=0-104857599 part0.bin
```

aws-perf-mcq-037.explanation: **The problem:** Millions of timestamped sensor readings per minute, time-windowed aggregations, and automatic aging of old data to cheaper storage. **Why Timestream:** it's the serverless time-series database — built for high-throughput timestamped ingestion, time-windowed SQL analytics (interpolation, smoothing), and automatic tiering from a memory store to a cheaper magnetic store by age. **Why the distractors fail:** general-purpose RDS strains at this write rate and needs hand-rolled partitioning/expiry; Neptune is graphs; Redis is a cache. **The signature:** sensor/metrics data + time-window queries → Timestream. **Common mistakes:** forcing time-series into a relational table, and building manual data-expiry pipelines.

aws-perf-mr-004.explanation: **The problem:** Users in Asia/Australia get slow page loads — both static assets and API calls — from a us-east-1 app. **Why the two answers:** distance is the enemy — CloudFront caches static content at edges near the users (and accelerates dynamic calls somewhat via backbone routing), while a *second Regional deployment* with Route 53 latency-based routing puts the *API itself* close to them, attacking both halves of the complaint. **Why both:** CloudFront fixes static + some dynamic; the regional stack fixes the API round trip. **Why the distractors fail:** bucket 'size' isn't a real dial; bigger instances and a different load balancer in Virginia don't shorten the 200+ ms round trip from Sydney. **Common mistakes:** scaling the origin Region instead of moving closer to users, and expecting CloudFront alone to fix API latency.

aws-perf-mcq-038.explanation: **The problem:** An RDS database on gp2 slows during sustained heavy I/O, and BurstBalance hits zero exactly when slowdowns start. **Why burst exhaustion:** gp2 earns burst credits at 3 IOPS/GB and spends them above baseline; sustained heavy I/O drains the bucket and performance collapses to baseline — the BurstBalance-hits-zero correlation is the textbook diagnosis. **The fix:** gp3 (decouples performance from size, flat 3,000 IOPS baseline, configurable higher) or Provisioned IOPS for the heaviest cases, sized for the sustained load. **Why the distractors fail:** RAM, connection pooling (RDS Proxy), and capacity are different problems with different metrics. **Common mistakes:** scaling instance RAM for an I/O-credit problem, and staying on gp2 for sustained high-IOPS workloads.

resources.label: AWS — gp2 vs gp3 / burst balance

aws-cost-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Audit logs must be kept 7 years; after 30 days they're rarely read and a 12-hour retrieval is acceptable. **Why Standard → Glacier Deep Archive via lifecycle:** Deep Archive is the cheapest class (~$1/TB-month) and its standard 12-hour retrieval is explicitly acceptable here; a lifecycle rule automates the transition after 30 days. **Why the distractors fail:** Standard for 7 years pays ~23× too much; Standard-IA still costs ~$12.5/TB-month; One Zone-IA trades AZ redundancy for a discount — risky for compliance data and still far pricier than Deep Archive. **The mapping:** rarely accessed + slow retrieval acceptable → Deep Archive. **Common mistakes:** leaving cold data in Standard, and using One Zone-IA for compliance-critical data.

aws-cost-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** A data lake's objects have *unpredictable* access — some hot for months, others never read again — and the team wants automatic optimization with no retrieval fees and no rules to maintain. **Why S3 Intelligent-Tiering:** it moves each object between access tiers automatically based on actual usage, charges *no retrieval fees*, and needs no lifecycle rules — only a small per-object monitoring charge. **Why the distractors fail:** static IA classes impose retrieval fees and penalize wrong guesses; Glacier classes are for genuinely archival data with retrieval delays. **The signal:** 'unknown/unpredictable access patterns' → Intelligent-Tiering. **Common mistakes:** using Standard-IA for unpredictable access (retrieval fees bite), and hand-maintaining lifecycle rules where Intelligent-Tiering is simpler.

aws-cost-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** A steady 24/7 workload committed for 3+ years, but instance families may change with modernization. **Why a 3-year Compute Savings Plan:** it gives up to ~66% off for a $/hour commitment while staying flexible across instance family, size, Region, OS — and even applies to Fargate and Lambda. **Why the distractors fail:** Standard RIs offer similar discounts but lock the family (conflicting with modernization); On-Demand leaves the discount unclaimed for steady usage; Spot can be reclaimed anytime (wrong for always-on production). **The pairing:** steady usage + flexibility → Compute Savings Plan; steady usage + fixed config → Standard RI. **Common mistakes:** buying family-locked Standard RIs when plans will change, and paying On-Demand for predictable 24/7 load.

aws-cost-mcq-004.explanation: **The problem:** A nightly, fault-tolerant, checkpointable batch job should cost the least. **Why Spot:** EC2 Spot uses spare capacity at up to 90% off, with the trade-off that AWS can reclaim instances on a two-minute warning — which checkpointable batch work absorbs easily. **Why the distractors fail:** RIs/Savings Plans suit steady 24/7 usage, not a few hours nightly; Dedicated Hosts solve licensing/compliance at the highest price; On-Demand is far pricier than Spot for interruptible work. **The signal words:** interruptible / fault-tolerant / flexible timing → Spot. **Common mistakes:** reserving capacity for part-time work, and avoiding Spot for genuinely interruptible jobs.

aws-cost-mr-001.explanation: **The problem:** A multi-account org needs monthly cost reporting by team and project. **Why the two answers:** define and *activate* cost allocation tags (e.g. `team`, `project`) on resources — tags don't appear in billing data until activated — then slice the tagged costs in Cost Explorer or the Cost and Usage Report, which consolidated billing aggregates across all member accounts. **Why both:** tagging produces the dimension; activation + analysis exposes it. **Why the distractors fail:** Shield Advanced (DDoS), IAM users, and Transfer Acceleration have nothing to do with cost reporting. **Common mistakes:** tagging but forgetting to *activate* the tags (no billing breakdown), and expecting per-account reporting without consolidated billing.

aws-cost-mcq-005.explanation: **The problem:** A team wants an automatic email when *forecasted* monthly spend exceeds $10,000, before month-end. **Why AWS Budgets:** it's the proactive tool — set a budget and alert on actual *or forecasted* spend crossing thresholds, optionally triggering actions (like applying a restrictive policy). **Why the distractors fail:** Cost Explorer is for interactive analysis after the fact; the invoice arrives too late by definition; Trusted Advisor flags optimization opportunities, not budget thresholds. **The pairing:** proactive threshold/forecast alerts → Budgets; interactive analysis → Cost Explorer. **Common mistakes:** using Cost Explorer for alerting, and waiting on the invoice to catch overruns.

aws-cost-mcq-006.explanation: **The problem:** A private-subnet app moves terabytes to/from S3 through a NAT gateway, racking up NAT data-processing charges. **Why a gateway VPC endpoint for S3:** it carries S3 (and DynamoDB) traffic over the AWS network with *no hourly or per-GB charge*, so the S3 traffic simply stops traversing the NAT gateway (~$0.045/GB processing) — it's the cost answer *and* the security answer. **Why the distractors fail:** a NAT *instance* trades managed reliability for marginal savings; Transfer Acceleration *adds* cost; moving to a public subnet changes security posture without addressing the charge. **Common mistakes:** routing S3 traffic through NAT when a free gateway endpoint exists, and reaching for interface endpoints (which do charge) for S3/DynamoDB.
aws-cost-mcq-006.example:
```bash
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --route-table-ids rtb-0private456
```

aws-cost-mcq-007.explanation: **The problem:** A public S3 dataset's downloads by thousands of external researchers drive up the *owner's* transfer bill. **Why Requester Pays:** it flips the billing — downloaders authenticate with their own AWS credentials and pay the request + data-transfer charges, while the owner keeps paying only storage. **Why the distractors fail:** storage class changes affect storage cost, not transfer; pre-signed URLs and throttling control *access*, but the owner still pays for every byte. **The mapping:** shift download cost to consumers → Requester Pays. **Common mistakes:** trying to reduce transfer cost by changing storage class, and assuming access controls change who pays.

aws-cost-mcq-008.explanation: **The problem:** A dev database is heavy during sprints, idle for weeks, and unpredictable. **Why Aurora Serverless v2:** it bills by Aurora Capacity Units that scale in fine-grained steps with actual load — scaling near zero between sprints — exactly matching 'intermittent, unpredictable'. **Why the distractors fail:** a large provisioned instance pays full price for idle weeks; a Reserved Instance doubles down on that commitment; Spot can be reclaimed mid-transaction, which databases tolerate badly. **The signal:** intermittent/spiky/unpredictable database load → Aurora Serverless v2. **Common mistakes:** provisioning a fixed large instance for bursty dev use, and reserving capacity for an intermittent workload.

aws-cost-mcq-009.explanation: **The problem:** Thousands of gp2 EBS volumes with ordinary needs cost more than necessary. **Why migrate gp2 → gp3:** gp3 is ~20% cheaper per GB and provides a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MBps baseline *independent of size* (gp2 ties IOPS to capacity), with performance configurable separately if needed — and migration is an online volume modification (no downtime). **Why the distractors fail:** io2 is the premium tier (more cost); st1 HDD doesn't fit random I/O; deleting volumes nightly isn't serious for persistent data. **The mapping:** cheaper general-purpose EBS with no performance loss → gp3. **Common mistakes:** staying on gp2 out of inertia, and over-provisioning to io2 for ordinary workloads.

aws-cost-mr-002.explanation: **The problem:** Dev EC2 instances run 24/7 but are used only weekday business hours, and most are over-provisioned. **Why the two answers (independent multipliers):** stopping instances outside business hours cuts running hours by ~75% (stopped instances don't bill for compute), and right-sizing down (per Compute Optimizer / Cost Explorer recommendations) cuts the rate for the hours that remain. **Why both:** fewer hours × cheaper-per-hour compounds the savings. **Why the distractors fail:** 3-year RIs for part-time, shrinking workloads lock in the waste; Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive model; doubling sizes increases spend on already-underutilized machines. **Common mistakes:** reserving capacity for part-time dev, and oversizing 'for headroom'.

aws-cost-mcq-010.explanation: **The problem:** An API at a few hundred sub-second requests/day runs on two always-on EC2 instances behind an ALB. **Why API Gateway + Lambda:** the workload is idle >99.9% of the time — the definition of a serverless fit; Lambda bills per invocation and per ms (with a permanent free tier that may cover this entirely), and API Gateway replaces the always-on ALB. **Why the distractors fail:** every EC2/ECS variant keeps paying for idle hours; an RI just discounts the waste. **The signal:** very low, spiky, idle-heavy traffic → serverless. **Common mistakes:** keeping always-on compute for near-idle APIs, and discounting waste with RIs instead of removing it.

aws-cost-mcq-011.explanation: **The problem:** A new DynamoDB table has wildly unpredictable traffic — near-zero for hours, then sudden spikes. **Why on-demand capacity mode:** it bills per request with no capacity planning and absorbs sudden spikes without pre-provisioning — near-zero idle hours cost near zero. **Why the distractors fail:** provisioning for peak pays for the spike 24/7; auto scaling reacts in minutes so unannounced spikes throttle first; reserved capacity commits to a baseline this workload doesn't have. **The crossover:** steady, predictable traffic eventually makes *provisioned* cheaper — the exam tests recognizing which side you're on. **Common mistakes:** provisioning for peak (paying for idle), and relying on auto scaling for sudden unannounced spikes.

aws-cost-mcq-012.explanation: **The problem:** The S3 bill shows storage charges that don't match visible objects, and the bucket gets many large uploads from unreliable clients. **Why abandoned incomplete multipart uploads:** parts of a multipart upload that's never completed or aborted sit invisibly — they don't appear in object listings but bill as storage indefinitely, and unreliable clients accumulate them fast. **The fix:** a lifecycle rule with `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` (e.g. after 7 days); Storage Lens and `ListMultipartUploads` reveal the backlog. **Why the distractors fail:** delete markers, access logs, and replication copies describe costs that are *visible* or intentional. **Common mistakes:** ignoring incomplete multipart cleanup, and hunting visible objects for phantom storage.

aws-cost-mcq-013.explanation: **The problem:** A containerized Linux workload on m5 (x86) wants better price-performance with minimal change. **Why Graviton (ARM):** Graviton instances (e.g. m7g) deliver up to ~40% better price-performance than comparable x86, and containerized Linux is the easiest migration — rebuild multi-arch images for arm64 and redeploy. **Why the distractors fail:** newer x86 generations help single-digit percentages; t3.micro is a size, not a strategy (undersizing throttles); Windows adds license cost. **Watch the constraint:** closed-source x86-only binaries block the move. **Common mistakes:** assuming x86-only dependencies can run on ARM, and chasing marginal gains from same-architecture upgrades.

aws-cost-mcq-014.explanation: **The problem:** A dev VPC has one NAT gateway per AZ (three), and dev tolerates downtime. **Why consolidate to one NAT gateway:** each NAT gateway bills hourly (~$32/month) plus per-GB processing, so three triple the hourly cost; dev environments that tolerate downtime can route all private subnets to a single NAT gateway — the documented cost optimization, with the explicit trade-off that an AZ failure breaks egress for the others. **Why the distractors fail:** internet gateways don't provide NAT for private instances; a fourth NAT gateway adds cost; public IPs change the security posture. **Why production differs:** prod keeps one NAT per AZ (availability + avoiding cross-AZ data charges). **Common mistakes:** consolidating NAT in production, and replacing NAT with an internet gateway.

aws-cost-mcq-015.explanation: **The problem:** A popular site serves large downloads directly from S3, generating big data-transfer-out charges. **Why CloudFront:** origin-to-CloudFront transfer is free, CloudFront's per-GB internet rates undercut S3's, caching means popular files leave the origin once instead of millions of times, and users download from nearby edges — cheaper *and* faster. **Why the distractors fail:** compression helps but doesn't change rates; Region arbitrage saves cents while adding latency; Transfer Acceleration is for *uploads* and adds cost. **The mapping:** reduce S3 internet egress cost for popular content → front with CloudFront. **Common mistakes:** serving heavy downloads straight from S3, and confusing Transfer Acceleration (uploads) with CDN delivery.

aws-cost-mr-003.explanation: **The problem:** A high-volume Lambda (already efficient code) dominates the serverless bill. **Why the two answers:** Lambda bills GB-seconds, so migrating to arm64 (Graviton) cuts the per-ms price ~20% (and often runs faster), and tuning the memory setting finds the point where added CPU shortens duration enough to lower memory × time (Lambda Power Tuning automates the sweep — sometimes *more* memory is cheaper). **Why both:** cheaper per-ms rate + optimal memory×duration. **Why the distractors fail:** timeout is a safety cap, not a billing factor; always-on provisioned concurrency *adds* an hourly charge; more invocations means more request fees and overhead. **Common mistakes:** raising the timeout to cut cost, and assuming lower memory is always cheaper.

aws-cost-mcq-016.explanation: **The problem:** Restore 500 TB from Glacier Flexible Retrieval for a review due in a week, with cost over speed. **Why bulk retrieval:** Flexible Retrieval offers three tiers — expedited (1–5 min, priciest), standard (3–5 h), and bulk (5–12 h, lowest cost, designed for large planned restores) — and a week of lead time makes bulk's window irrelevant. **Why the distractors fail:** expedited at 500 TB maximizes spend for unneeded speed; provisioned capacity exists to guarantee *expedited* throughput; 'copy to Standard first' still performs a retrieval underneath. **The mapping:** large planned restore, cost-sensitive → bulk retrieval. **Common mistakes:** paying for expedited when time allows bulk, and thinking a copy avoids the retrieval cost.

aws-cost-mcq-017.explanation: **The problem:** Internal tools average 5% CPU with brief bursts to 60%, on m5.large. **Why T-family burstable instances:** they price for a low CPU baseline and accrue credits while idle to spend during bursts — a 5%-average workload runs comfortably and costs notably less than the equivalent m5. **Why the distractors fail:** C (compute) and R (memory) target sustained heavy use; P (GPU) is for ML/graphics. **Watch the failure mode (also tested):** sustained high CPU drains credits and throttles to baseline unless `unlimited` mode is on — which can quietly cost more than a fixed-performance instance. **Common mistakes:** running steady high-CPU work on T instances, and ignoring unlimited-mode charges.

aws-cost-mcq-018.explanation: **The problem:** A Spot fleet on a *single* instance type suffers frequent simultaneous interruptions when that pool is reclaimed. **Why a mixed-instances policy + capacity-optimized:** Spot interruptions happen per *capacity pool* (instance type × AZ), so diversifying across many types and AZs means one pool's reclamation takes out only a slice of the fleet, and the capacity-optimized allocation strategy launches into the deepest pools, statistically reducing interruptions. **Why the distractors fail:** 'bidding' higher doesn't help (the strategy is capacity-driven; you pay the market price); full On-Demand forfeits ~90% savings; one AZ is maximum blast radius. **Common mistakes:** running Spot on a single type/AZ, and thinking a higher max price reduces interruptions.

aws-cost-mcq-019.explanation: **The problem:** Thousands of ad-hoc EBS snapshots accumulate; the policy should be daily snapshots, keep 14 days, then auto-delete. **Why Data Lifecycle Manager:** DLM automates EBS snapshot (and AMI) lifecycles — tag-targeted policies create snapshots on schedule and expire them by age or count, exactly 'daily, keep 14, delete'. (AWS Backup is the broader alternative when one plan spans multiple services.) **Why the distractors fail:** S3 lifecycle rules don't govern EBS snapshots (even though snapshots live in S3 internally); Trusted Advisor reports, it doesn't delete; manual cleanup is how the problem grew. **Common mistakes:** trying S3 lifecycle rules on snapshots, and relying on manual cleanup.

aws-cost-mr-004.explanation: **The problem:** A monthly review should surface idle/underused resources with concrete recommendations. **Why the two tools:** Trusted Advisor's cost checks flag idle resources (unassociated Elastic IPs, idle load balancers, low-utilization instances, unattached volumes), and Compute Optimizer goes deeper on sizing — ML over CloudWatch metrics yields specific instance-type recommendations (also for EBS, Lambda, ECS). **Why both:** 'what's wasted' (Trusted Advisor) + 'what's oversized' (Compute Optimizer). **Why the distractors fail:** CloudTrail is an API audit log; Route 53 health checks test endpoints; Artifact downloads compliance documents. **Common mistakes:** expecting CloudTrail to surface waste, and using only one of the two tools.

aws-cost-mcq-020.explanation: **The problem:** Non-prod RDS instances run 24/7 but are used only weekday business hours; snapshots must be retained. **Why stop them outside business hours:** stopped RDS instances stop billing instance-hours (storage and backups still bill), cutting runtime ~75%. **The caveat worth knowing:** RDS auto-starts stopped instances after 7 days, so a scheduler must re-stop them. **Why the distractors fail:** delete/recreate loses configuration and takes time daily; Multi-AZ *doubles* instance cost; io2 raises storage cost. **Pair with right-sizing** for the remaining hours. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the 7-day auto-start, and enabling Multi-AZ on cost-sensitive non-prod.

resources.label: AWS — Stopping an RDS instance temporarily

aws-cost-mcq-021.explanation: **The problem:** Medical images are written once, read ~quarterly, but must load in milliseconds when opened. **Why S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval:** it's the archive class with *millisecond* access — about 68% cheaper storage than Standard-IA for data touched roughly once a quarter, trading a higher per-GB retrieval fee that rare access keeps small. **Why the distractors fail:** Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive take minutes to hours (fails the doctor's click); Standard pays full price for data idle 99.9% of the time. **The mapping:** rarely accessed but instant when needed → Glacier Instant Retrieval. **Common mistakes:** using Flexible/Deep Archive where millisecond access is required, and leaving rarely-read data in Standard.

aws-cost-mcq-022.explanation: **The problem:** Thumbnails that can be regenerated from originals are accessed infrequently — what's the cheapest fit? **Why S3 One Zone-IA:** it stores data in a single AZ at ~20% less than Standard-IA; the trade-off (data loss if that AZ is destroyed) is precisely acceptable when the data is derivative/re-creatable (thumbnails, transcodes, replicas of on-prem data). **Why the distractors fail:** Standard-IA and Standard pay for multi-AZ redundancy this data doesn't need; Deep Archive's hours-long retrieval can't serve images. **The cue:** re-creatable/derivative + infrequent → One Zone-IA; primary/irreplaceable → multi-AZ classes. **Common mistakes:** using One Zone-IA for irreplaceable data, and overpaying for redundancy on regenerable data.

aws-cost-mcq-023.explanation: **The problem:** An EFS file system bills entirely at Standard rate though most files are untouched for months, and access patterns can't change for users. **Why EFS lifecycle management:** it automatically moves files unaccessed for a configured window into EFS IA (up to ~92% cheaper per GB; an Archive class goes further) and transparently moves them back on access — same paths, same NFS semantics, users notice only a slightly slower first read. **Why the distractors fail:** instance store is ephemeral local disk; read-only mounts and mount-target counts don't affect storage rates. **The mapping:** cold files on EFS, transparent savings → lifecycle management to IA. **Common mistakes:** leaving all EFS data in Standard, and assuming IA changes the user experience.

aws-cost-mcq-024.explanation: **The problem:** DynamoDB session items are useless after 24h but accumulate, and scheduled scan-and-delete consumes write capacity. **Why DynamoDB TTL:** set an epoch-timestamp attribute and DynamoDB deletes expired items in a background process consuming *no write capacity* and costing nothing — built for sessions, tokens, and event data with natural lifetimes (deletions happen within a window, typically minutes to ~48h). **Why the distractors fail:** the scan-and-delete Lambda pays RCUs for the scan and WCUs per delete (the exact cost being eliminated); daily table recreation drops *all* data; capacity-mode changes billing math, not data volume. **Common mistakes:** building scan-and-delete jobs, and expecting TTL deletions to be instantaneous.

aws-cost-mcq-025.explanation: **The problem:** The CloudWatch Logs bill climbs because log groups retain every line forever. **Why set retention policies:** CloudWatch Logs groups default to **Never Expire** — a quiet cost accumulator; setting retention (e.g. 30–90 days per compliance needs) expires old events automatically. For logs needed long-term, export to S3 and lifecycle them into Glacier tiers at a fraction of the price. **Why the distractors fail:** turning logging off trades cost for blindness; printing to stdout without CloudWatch and creating a second account dodge rather than manage the data. **Common mistakes:** leaving log groups on Never Expire, and disabling logging to save money.

aws-cost-mcq-026.explanation: **The problem:** Finance wants alerts when any service deviates abnormally from its historical spending pattern (e.g. a misconfigured job tripling NAT costs overnight) without per-service thresholds. **Why Cost Anomaly Detection:** it learns each monitored segment's spending pattern with ML and alerts on deviations — no thresholds to define or maintain — with root-cause hints (service, account, usage type). **Why the distractors fail:** Budgets are great for *known* limits, but a tripled NAT bill can hide inside a healthy monthly total until too late; weekly manual checks find anomalies after days; Trusted Advisor flags static optimization, not spend deviations. **The pairing:** known limits → Budgets; unknown anomalies → Cost Anomaly Detection. **Common mistakes:** relying only on a fixed monthly Budget to catch spikes.

aws-cost-mcq-027.explanation: **The problem:** In a 30-account org with consolidated billing, the platform team buys Savings Plans in the management account; a member account starts matching compute — does the discount apply? **Why it applies org-wide:** under consolidated billing, Savings Plans and RI discounts float across the organization — the commitment first covers the purchasing account's usage, then any member account's matching usage; volume-tiered pricing (S3, data transfer) also aggregates across accounts. **Why the distractors fail:** discounts aren't confined to the purchasing account, and accounts don't each need their own plans. **The nuance:** discount sharing can be *disabled* per account when chargeback models require it. **Common mistakes:** buying duplicate plans per account, and assuming discounts are account-local.

aws-cost-mcq-028.explanation: **The problem:** Per-socket Windows/SQL Server BYOL licenses require visibility and control of the physical sockets/cores the software runs on. **Why Dedicated Hosts:** you get a physical server allocated to you with socket/core visibility, placement control (host affinity), and License Manager tracking — satisfying socket-bound license terms. **The exam trap:** Dedicated *Instances* are also single-tenant hardware but *without* socket visibility or placement control, which per-socket licenses require. **Why the other distractors fail:** standard On-Demand with 'license tags' documents nothing binding; Spot on isolated hardware doesn't address licensing terms. **The mapping:** per-socket/core BYOL → Dedicated Hosts. **Common mistakes:** choosing Dedicated Instances for socket-bound licenses, and thinking tags satisfy license terms.

aws-cost-mcq-029.explanation: **The problem:** A Fargate batch service tolerates interruptions and auto-reruns failed tasks — cut its compute cost. **Why Fargate Spot:** it runs tasks on spare capacity at up to ~70% off with a two-minute interruption warning — the same bargain as EC2 Spot, without managing instances; capacity providers can mix regular Fargate (must-run baseline) with Spot (the bulk). **Why the distractors fail:** bigger Fargate sizes bill proportionally more; ECS on On-Demand EC2 reintroduces fleet ops; Lambda has its own limits and pricing model. **The signal:** interruption-tolerant, retry-capable containers → Fargate Spot. **Common mistakes:** running interruptible batch on full-price Fargate, and reintroducing EC2 fleet management for cost.

aws-cost-mcq-030.explanation: **The problem:** A storage team needs org-wide S3 visibility — object counts, storage-class distribution, incomplete multipart uploads, and recommendations — in one dashboard across 25 accounts. **Why S3 Storage Lens:** it aggregates S3 metrics across an entire organization into dashboards (storage by class, object counts, incomplete-multipart bytes, replication/encryption coverage) with contextual recommendations; advanced metrics add prefix-level depth. **Why the distractors fail:** access logs record requests (not inventory) and parsing them across 25 accounts is a project; billing alarms watch totals; per-bucket Inventory reports are the raw material Storage Lens already rolls up. **The mapping:** org-wide S3 usage analytics → Storage Lens. **Common mistakes:** stitching together per-bucket Inventory by hand, and using billing alarms for usage analytics.

aws-cost-mr-005.explanation: **The problem:** ~1 TB/day of logs — queried frequently for 2 weeks, occasionally to 90 days, deleted after 1 year. **Why the two lifecycle actions:** lifecycle rules have exactly two action types — *transitions* and *expirations* — and this pattern maps cleanly: Standard for the hot 2 weeks, Standard-IA at ~14–30 days, a Glacier tier at 90, expire at 365 (which also enforces the retention limit automatically). **Why both:** transitions cut storage cost as access drops; expiration deletes (and enforces retention). **Why the distractors fail:** replication *doubles* cost; Transfer Acceleration is unrelated; format conversion helps query cost but isn't a lifecycle action. **Common mistakes:** keeping logs in Standard the whole year, and not setting an expiration to enforce retention.

aws-cost-mr-006.explanation: **The problem:** 10 instances 24/7 (steady baseline) plus up to 30 extra during unpredictable, fault-tolerant bursts — minimize cost. **Why the two answers (layered purchasing):** cover the always-on baseline with a Savings Plan or RIs (predictable → ~60–70% savings), and serve the burst capacity from Spot in an Auto Scaling group (unpredictable + fault-tolerant → up to 90% off, scaled only when needed). **Why both:** match commitment to certainty — commit the baseline, Spot the bursts. **Why the distractors fail:** reserving all 40 pays for 30 mostly-idle commitments; full On-Demand leaves every discount unclaimed; Spot for the *baseline* risks losing capacity the workload must always have. **Common mistakes:** reserving peak capacity, and putting must-run baseline load on Spot.
